Meet Your Faculty Shamini Ayyadhury (She/Her) Founder, CEO Panoramics - A Vision Inc.  Toronto, Ontario, Canadav Shamini.Ayyadhury@panoramics-a-vision.com Dr. Shamini Ayyadhury is the Founder and CEO of Panoramics - A Vision, a life sciences corporation dedicated to biological topography, and the Chair of True North Spatial, Canada’s national summit on spatial and single-cell biology. Through The Panoramic Chapters, she collaborates with the Canadian Bioinformatics Workshops to develop meaningful, creative workshops for the spatial and single-cell community. She is a Scientific Associate at the University Health Network and was previously a postdoctoral fellow in spatial biology and computer vision at the University of Toronto. She holds a PhD in Neuroscience from McGill University, a Master’s from Imperial College London, and a BSc from the National University of Singapore. Outside science, she boxes and makes art. Alyona Ivanova (She/Her) PhD Candidate University of Toronto, The Hospital for Sick Children Toronto, Ontario, Canada alyona.ivanova@mail.utoronto.ca Alyona is a graduate student at the University of Toronto pursuing PhD in Medical Sciences. Her research focuses on identifying novel therapies for targeting chemo-resistance in glioblastoma using spatial ’omics technologies. She works in close collaboration with clinicians, neuropathologists, scientists bridging the gap between clinical practice and fundamental lab research. Alyona is a Creative Director of Panoramics - A Vision, and an Executive Editor and Director of Distribution of the Institute of Medical Sciences Magazine. Melanie Peralta (She/Her) Laboratory manager - MLT Mount Sinai Hospital Toronto, Ontario, Canada melanie.peralta@sinaihealth.ca Melanie is a Laboratory Manager at Mount Sinai Services. She is a Certified Medical Laboratory Technologist in good standing with the College of Medical Laboratory Technologists of Ontario. Her specialties are in Histology and Immunohistochemistry. In the past 25 years she has worked closely with researchers from UHN, U of T, LTRI, Mount Sinai Hospital and other institutions. Her work has been published in a few journals and presentations which include RNAscope, Visium, Visium HD and Xenium. She has also worked as a lab instructor for The Michener Institute bridging program for international laboratory technologists. Her passion in teaching, research, and leadership is ensuring that knowledge is shared among future researchers in years to come. #### Zhibin Lu (He/Him) Senior Manager and Architect, Digital Research University Health Network Toronto, Ontario, Canada zhibin@gmail.com Zhibin Lu is a senior manager at University Health Network Digital. He is responsible for UHN HPC operations and scientific software. He manages two HPC clusters at UHN, including system administration, user management, and maintenance of bioinformatics tools for HPC4health. He is a member of the Digital Research Alliance of Canada Bioinformatics National Team and Scheduling National Team. Module 2 Understanding your inputs and outputs Lecture Lab Canadian Bioinformatics Workshops & Enlighten-me Chapter (Panoramics - A Vision) Instruction : Shamini Ayyadhury, PhD Code preparation: Shamini Ayyadhury, PhD Date : 12th September, 2026 contact : shamini.ayyadhury@panoramics-a-vision.com A. Spatial workflows from different vendors result in different saved formats. B. Before we analyse anything, we need to know what we actually are getting and to understand the file structure and components that will be valuable for analysis. 0. Setup ACTIVATE CONDA ENVIRONMENT - spatial import scanpy as sc import anndata as ad import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import os import sys import pathlib import zarr import h5py import tarfile DIR+FILEPATHS ROOT_DATA_DIR = ‘/media/cbwdata/’ DATA_DIR_PATH = os.path.join(ROOT_DATA_DIR, ‘CourseData/datasets’) WORKING_DIR_PATH = os.path.join(ROOT_DATA_DIR, ‘workspace’) SRC_FOLDER = os.path.join(WORKING_DIR_PATH, ‘SRC’) DST_FOLDER = os.path.join(WORKING_DIR_PATH, ‘DST’) DST_FOLDER_MODULE2 = os.path.join(DST_FOLDER, ‘module2’) os.makedirs(DST_FOLDER, exist_ok=True) os.makedirs(DST_FOLDER_MODULE2, exist_ok=True) - Small helper so we can print a folder tree. Highlighted files are the ones we will actually open. - Usually these will be executed on the command line. def list_files_tree(data_dir_path, depth=0, bold_highlight=False, list_to_bold_highlight=None): if list_to_bold_highlight is None: list_to_bold_highlight = [] #print only once if depth == 0: print(f'TREE STRUCTURE OF OUTPUT DIRECTORY FOR {os.path.basename(data_dir_path)}') ELBOW, SPACE = '|_', ' ' print(SPACE * depth, ELBOW , os.path.basename(data_dir_path)) if os.path.isdir(data_dir_path): contents = os.listdir(data_dir_path) for content in contents: if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(data_dir_path, content)): list_files_tree(os.path.join(data_dir_path, content), depth=depth+1, bold_highlight=bold_highlight, list_to_bold_highlight=list_to_bold_highlight) else: if bold_highlight and content in list_to_bold_highlight: print(SPACE * (depth+1), ELBOW , "\033[1;100m", content, "\033[0m") else: print(SPACE * (depth+1), ELBOW , content) 1. In-class: Xenium (imaging / single-molecule) 10x Xenium. Human colon cancer FFPE. Useful files: | FILE | DESCRIPTION | |—|—| | - transcripts.csv.gz / transcripts.parquet | one row per transcript (gene, x, y, z, cell assignment) | - cells.csv.gz / cells.parquet | one row per cell (centroid, counts) | - cell_boundaries.parquet | cell polygons | - cells.zarr.zip | masks and polygons in zarr | - cell_feature_matrix.h5 | cell x gene expression (10x HDF5) list_files = [‘cells.parquet’, ‘cells.csv.gz’, ‘cells.zarr.zip’, ‘transcripts.parquet’, ‘transcripts.csv.gz’, ‘cell_boundaries.parquet’, ‘cell_feature_matrix.h5’] list_files_tree(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘xenium’), depth=0, bold_highlight=True, list_to_bold_highlight=list_files) Transcripts Do not load the whole file. nrows is enough to see the columns. Let’s take a look at the transcripts file only see first 21 rows. So don’t load the whole file into memory use pandas to load the first 21 rows transcripts = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘xenium’, ‘original’, ‘transcripts.csv.gz’), nrows=21) print(“QUESTIONS TO PONDER:”) print(“1. What do you see in the transcripts file?”) print(“2. What does the column ‘cell_id’ mean? And what defines if a transcript belongs to a cell? - think what defines a cell in a Xenium experiment”) print(“3. What other columns are there that you think might be important?”) display(transcripts) Each row is one decoded transcript. cell_id can be UNASSIGNED - not every molecule falls inside a segmented cell. - We will see in Module 4 - how these re-assignments can happen. Cells - when the transcripts have been summed per cell. cells = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘xenium’, ‘original’, ‘cells.csv.gz’), nrows=12) ’’‘———————————–’’’ print(“QUESTIONS TO PONDER:”) print(“1. What do you see in the cells file?”) print(“2. What does the column ‘cell_id’ mean? And what does it mean per row?”) print(“3. Control probes - what relevance they have here?”) print(“4. What other columns are there that you think might be important?”) print(“5. Coordinates are in what scale?”) display(cells) cells is the per-cell summary: centroid, transcript counts, control probe counts. This is what is ingested into standard seurat and anndata containers/objects. #### Other support files Zarr zip: cell ids, segmentation masks, and polygon vertices. We only print the tree - do not load the full masks. - These are very memory efficient, do lazy loading. - It might take a bit of learning curve. Expression matrix. 10x HDF5: sparse CSR (data, indices, indptr) plus barcodes and features. 2. Self: CosMx (imaging / single-molecule) Same idea as Xenium, different filenames. Nanostring / Bruker CosMx, human hippocampus WTX. Useful files: S0_tx_file.csv.gz — transcripts (molecule table). Listed in md5sums.txt; this copy of the folder may not include it S0_metadata_file.csv.gz — per-cell metadata (centroids, area, RNA counts) S0_exprMat_file.csv.gz — dense cell x gene matrix S0-polygons.csv.gz — cell outlines S0_fov_positions_file.csv.gz — FOV anchors on the slide list_files = [‘S0_tx_file.csv.gz’, ‘S0_metadata_file.csv.gz’, ‘S0_exprMat_file.csv.gz’, ‘S0-polygons.csv.gz’, ‘S0_fov_positions_file.csv.gz’] list_files_tree(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘cosmx’), depth=0, bold_highlight=True, list_to_bold_highlight=list_files) Transcripts The S0_tx_file.csv.gz - this is the CosMx equivalent of Xenium transcripts.csv.gz. Columns: fov, cell_ID, x_global_px, y_global_px, target, CellComp. Let’s take a look at the transcripts file only see first 21 rows. So don’t load the whole file into memory use pandas to load the first 21 rows TX_FILE_PATH = os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘cosmx’, ‘S0_tx_file.csv.gz’) if os.path.exists(TX_FILE_PATH): transcripts = pd.read_csv(TX_FILE_PATH, nrows=21) display(transcripts) else: print(‘S0_tx_file.csv.gz is not in the folder (it is listed in md5sums.txt).’) print(‘Expected columns: fov, cell_ID, cell, x_local_px, y_local_px, x_global_px, y_global_px, z, target, CellComp’) cells = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘cosmx’, ‘original’,‘S0_metadata_file.csv.gz’), nrows=21) cells Dense expression matrix: fov, cell_ID, then one column per gene. Only peek a few rows and a few columns. expression file given as a csv.gz. read first 21 rows and first 21 columns expression = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘cosmx’, ‘original’,‘S0_exprMat_file.csv.gz’), nrows=21) expression.iloc[:, :21] cell polygons and FOV positions polygons = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘cosmx’, ‘original’,‘S0-polygons.csv.gz’), nrows=21) fovs = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘cosmx’, ‘original’,‘S0_fov_positions_file.csv.gz’), nrows=21) print(‘— polygons —’) display(polygons) print(‘— fov positions —’) display(fovs) 3. Self: Visium HD (spot / bin-based) 10x Visium HD, human colon cancer. Square bins at 2 / 8 / 16 µm, not single cells. Useful files: | FILE | DESCRIPTION | |—|—| | - *_binned_outputs.tar.gz — the analysis folder (square_002um, square_008um, …), each with a 10x matrix + spatial/ | - *_feature_slice.h5 — gene-wise sparse slices over the grid | - *_molecule_info.h5 — molecule-level UMI table | - *_probe_set.csv — probe panel | - *_metrics_summary.csv — run metrics now let’s look at visiumHD list_files = [“Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)_tissue_image.btf”, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)_feature_slice.h5”, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)_molecule_info.h5”, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)_binned_outputs.tar.gz”, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)_probe_set.csv”, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)_metrics_summary.csv”] list_files_tree(os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, “visiumHD”, ‘original’, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)”), depth=0, bold_highlight=True, list_to_bold_highlight=list_files) You should see square_002um, square_008um, each with filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5 and spatial/. BINNED_TAR = os.path.join(DATA_DIR_PATH, ‘visiumHD’, ‘original’, “Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Human Lymph Node (FFPE)”, ‘Visium_HD_Human_Lymph_Node_FFPE_binned_outputs.tar.gz’) with tarfile.open(BINNED_TAR, ‘r:gz’) as tar: for i, member in enumerate(tar): print(member.name) if i >= 40: print(‘…’) break The h5 file contains a compressed, hierarchical matrix of the spatial gene expression data.
